
# Epilogue: beyond comparing groups

The tests above answer a descriptive question: *is there a difference between groups?*
Data mining asks a different one: *can we use what we measured to predict or to group?*
With the snoring data, a logistic regression could estimate the probability that a person
snores from their age, BMI, alcohol and tobacco consumption, and tell us which factors
contribute once the others are taken into account, something that separate two-group tests
cannot do. Methods such as PCA or clustering go further and look for profiles of
individuals without any outcome chosen in advance. These tools are only useful if we know
why we use them: a prediction model needs a clear question, enough participants for the
number of predictors, and validation on new data, otherwise it only describes the noise of
one sample. In clinical or sport research, the value lies less in the algorithm than in the
decision it supports, such as identifying patients who would benefit most from
rehabilitation.
